questions.question: When did the Constitution of India come into force?
questions.explanation: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came fully into force on 26 January 1950, which we celebrate as Republic Day.

questions.question: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
questions.explanation: Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee. Dr Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Constituent Assembly.
questions.reference: Constituent Assembly of India, Drafting Committee (constituted 29 August 1947)

questions.question: Which Article says "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States"?
questions.explanation: Article 1 gives the name of the country and describes it as a Union of States. Article 3 deals with forming new States.

questions.question: What is the minimum age to be elected President of India?
questions.explanation: A candidate for President must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old, and qualified to be elected to the Lok Sabha.

questions.question: Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment, 1976?
questions.explanation: The 42nd Amendment added 'Socialist' and 'Secular', and changed 'unity of the Nation' to 'unity and integrity of the Nation'.

questions.question: What is the normal term of the Lok Sabha?
questions.explanation: The Lok Sabha lasts five years from its first meeting unless dissolved earlier. Only during an Emergency can Parliament extend it, one year at a time.

questions.question: Which Article gives the President the power to grant pardons, including in death sentence cases?
questions.explanation: Article 72 lets the President pardon, remit or commute sentences, including death sentences. Article 161 gives Governors a similar power.

questions.question: Whose decision is final on whether a Bill is a Money Bill?
questions.explanation: Article 110(3) makes the Speaker's decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill final.

questions.question: If the Rajya Sabha does not return a Money Bill within how many days is it deemed passed?
questions.explanation: The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes to a Money Bill. If it does not return the Bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed by both Houses.

questions.question: Which Amendment replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" as a ground for National Emergency?
questions.explanation: After the 1975 Emergency, the 44th Amendment narrowed Article 352 so that only war, external aggression or armed rebellion can justify it.
questions.reference: Article 352(1), as amended by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978

questions.question: At what age does a Supreme Court judge retire?
questions.explanation: Supreme Court judges hold office until 65. High Court judges retire at 62 under Article 217(1).

questions.question: Which Article provides for a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament?
questions.explanation: The President may call a joint sitting to resolve a deadlock on an ordinary Bill. It is not available for Money Bills or Constitution amendments.

questions.question: What was the bench strength and majority in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)?
questions.explanation: A 13-judge bench held by 7:6 that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot destroy its basic structure.
questions.reference: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, (1973) 4 SCC 225

questions.question: Which case struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 inserted by the 42nd Amendment?
options: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981)
questions.explanation: Minerva Mills held that limited amending power and judicial review are part of the basic structure, so Parliament cannot give itself unlimited power.
questions.reference: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625

questions.question: In I.R. Coelho (2007), laws added to the Ninth Schedule after which date can be tested against the basic structure?
questions.explanation: 24 April 1973 is the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment. Ninth Schedule laws added after it are open to basic structure review.
questions.reference: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2007) 2 SCC 1

questions.question: In which case did the Supreme Court strike down the 99th Amendment creating the NJAC?
options: SC Advocates-on-Record Assn. v. Union of India (2015)
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981)
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
questions.explanation: The Fourth Judges Case (2015) held the NJAC unconstitutional as it hurt judicial independence, a basic feature, and restored the collegium system.
questions.reference: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn. v. Union of India, (2016) 5 SCC 1

questions.question: An amendment changing the representation of States in Parliament needs, besides a special majority:
options: Ratification by two-thirds of the States
An advisory opinion of the Supreme Court
Ratification by at least half the State Legislatures
questions.explanation: Under the proviso to Article 368(2), amendments to federal features, such as representation of States in Parliament, need ratification by half the States.

questions.question: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), where must a government's majority be tested?
options: At Raj Bhavan before the Governor
On the floor of the House
questions.explanation: Bommai held that majority is proved by a floor test, not the Governor's opinion, and that President's Rule under Article 356 is open to judicial review.
questions.reference: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, (1994) 3 SCC 1

questions.question: Which Article abolishes "untouchability"?
questions.explanation: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Enforcing any disability arising from it is an offence.

questions.question: The right to free and compulsory education covers children of which age group?
questions.explanation: Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment in 2002, makes free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 a Fundamental Right.

questions.question: Which Article protects the right to life and personal liberty?
questions.explanation: Article 21 says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. It applies to everyone, not just citizens.

questions.question: In which Article are the Fundamental Duties of citizens listed?
questions.explanation: Fundamental Duties were added in Part IVA (Article 51A) by the 42nd Amendment, 1976. There are now 11 duties.

questions.question: Which right did Dr B.R. Ambedkar call the "heart and soul" of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Article 32 lets a person go directly to the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights. Ambedkar called it the very soul and heart of the Constitution.
questions.reference: Article 32, Constitution of India; Constituent Assembly Debates, 9 December 1948

questions.question: Which Article guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws?
questions.explanation: Article 14 bars the State from denying any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws within India.

questions.question: Which writ is issued to free a person who is unlawfully detained?
questions.explanation: Habeas corpus means 'you may have the body'. The court orders the detainer to produce the person and justify the detention; it can issue even against private persons.

questions.question: Which writ questions a person's legal right to hold a public office?
questions.explanation: Quo warranto ('by what authority') asks the holder of a public office to show their legal right to it and can remove a usurper.

questions.question: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) held that procedure under Article 21 must be:
questions.explanation: The Court held that any law depriving liberty must be just, fair and reasonable, and read Articles 14, 19 and 21 together.
questions.reference: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, (1978) 1 SCC 248

questions.question: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the nine-judge bench held that privacy is:
options: A Fundamental Right under Article 21 and Part III
Only a statutory right under the IT Act
questions.explanation: The Court unanimously held that privacy is intrinsic to life and liberty under Article 21 and to the freedoms in Part III.
questions.reference: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1

questions.question: How is the writ power of High Courts under Article 226 wider than Article 32?
options: It applies only to Fundamental Rights
It covers any other purpose, not just Fundamental Rights
It applies only against private bodies
It applies only in criminal matters
questions.explanation: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose', such as enforcing legal rights.

questions.question: Which Directive Principle asks the State to provide free legal aid?
questions.explanation: Article 39A, added by the 42nd Amendment, directs equal justice and free legal aid. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 gives effect to it.

questions.question: Puttaswamy (2017) overruled which earlier rulings to the extent they denied a right to privacy?
questions.explanation: The nine-judge bench overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh insofar as they held there is no constitutional right to privacy.
questions.reference: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1

questions.question: Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) held that involuntary narco-analysis violates:
questions.explanation: Forcing narco-analysis, polygraph or brain-mapping tests breaches the right against self-incrimination and personal liberty.
questions.reference: Selvi v. State of Karnataka, (2010) 7 SCC 263

questions.question: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) generally capped total reservations at:
questions.explanation: The nine-judge bench set a 50% ceiling save in extraordinary situations and required exclusion of the 'creamy layer' among backward classes.
questions.reference: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India, 1992 Supp (3) SCC 217

questions.question: Under Article 22(4), preventive detention beyond how long needs an Advisory Board's opinion?
questions.explanation: No preventive detention law can authorise detention beyond three months unless an Advisory Board reports sufficient cause.

questions.question: During an Emergency, enforcement of which Articles cannot be suspended under Article 359?
questions.explanation: The 44th Amendment, 1978 barred suspension of Articles 20 and 21, undoing the effect of ADM Jabalpur (1976).
questions.reference: Article 359(1), as amended by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978

questions.question: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) held that speech and trade through the internet are protected by:
questions.explanation: The Court held these freedoms extend to the internet, so internet shutdown orders must be necessary, proportionate and open to judicial review.
questions.reference: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637

questions.question: From which date did the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replace the Indian Penal Code?
questions.explanation: The BNS, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024 and replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860, along with the new BNSS and BSA.

questions.question: Which BNS section punishes theft?
questions.explanation: Theft is defined and punished in BNS Section 303 (old IPC 379). BNS 302 deals with wounding religious feelings, and 318 is cheating.

questions.question: Which new type of punishment did the BNS introduce?
questions.explanation: Section 4(f) adds community service as a punishment for some minor offences, such as small first-time theft and defamation.

questions.question: Under the BNS, a "child" means a person below what age?
questions.explanation: The BNS defines a child as any person below eighteen years of age.

questions.question: Which BNS section prescribes the punishment for murder?
questions.explanation: Section 103 punishes murder with death or life imprisonment and fine (old IPC 302). Section 101 only defines murder.

questions.question: Nothing done by a child below what age is an offence under the BNS?
questions.explanation: The law presumes a child under seven cannot form criminal intent, so their acts are not offences (old IPC 82).

questions.question: Suddenly grabbing a chain or phone from someone is now a separate offence called:
questions.explanation: BNS Section 304 makes snatching a distinct form of theft: suddenly, quickly or forcibly seizing movable property from a person.

questions.question: For a "dowry death" under BNS Section 80, the woman must die within how many years of marriage?
questions.explanation: Dowry death needs an unnatural death within seven years of marriage after dowry-related cruelty. Punishment is 7 years to life (old IPC 304B).

questions.question: Which BNS section punishes cruelty to a woman by her husband or his relatives (old IPC 498A)?
questions.explanation: Section 85 punishes such cruelty with up to three years and fine. Section 86 explains what 'cruelty' means.

questions.question: BNS Section 103(2) covers murder by a group on grounds like race or caste. How big must the group be?
questions.explanation: This new provision targets mob lynching: each member of a group of five or more is punished with death or life imprisonment and fine.

questions.question: Sedition (IPC 124A) was dropped. Which BNS section punishes acts endangering India's sovereignty, unity and integrity?
questions.explanation: Section 152 punishes acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India. Section 147 is waging war; 113 is terrorist act.

questions.question: Sexual intercourse on a false promise of marriage, not amounting to rape, is punished under:
questions.explanation: Section 69 is a new offence covering intercourse by deceitful means, such as a false promise of marriage or job; up to 10 years and fine.

questions.question: When can theft be punished with community service under BNS Section 303(2)?
options: First conviction, value under ₹5,000, property restored
questions.explanation: The proviso allows community service only for a first-time offender where the stolen property is worth under ₹5,000 and is returned or its value paid.

questions.question: Which BNS section defines and punishes "organised crime" by a crime syndicate?
questions.explanation: Section 111 covers continuing unlawful activity by a syndicate for material benefit. Section 112 is petty organised crime; 113 is terrorist act.

questions.question: In which BNS section are the cases where private defence of the body extends to causing death listed?
questions.explanation: Section 38 (old IPC 100) lists grave threats like fear of death, rape or kidnapping. Section 41 is the equivalent rule for defence of property.

questions.question: Which IPC offence, struck down in Joseph Shine (2018), has no counterpart in the BNS?
questions.explanation: Joseph Shine held IPC 497 unconstitutional and the BNS did not re-enact it. Bigamy (BNS 82) and cruelty (BNS 85) remain offences.
questions.reference: Joseph Shine v. Union of India, (2019) 3 SCC 39; Chapter V, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

questions.question: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (old IPC 304) is punished under which BNS section?
questions.explanation: Section 105 punishes it. Section 100 defines culpable homicide, 106 covers death by negligence and 110 is attempt to commit culpable homicide.

questions.question: Under BNS Section 106(1), the maximum sentence for a registered doctor causing death by negligence during a procedure is:
questions.explanation: Death by negligence generally carries up to 5 years, but for a registered medical practitioner during a medical procedure the maximum is 2 years.

questions.question: A "Zero FIR" means the police must register an FIR for a cognizable offence:
options: Only if it happened in their area
questions.explanation: Police must record information of a cognizable offence irrespective of where it happened, and then transfer it to the police station with jurisdiction.

questions.question: Within how many days must you sign a complaint sent electronically (e-FIR) for it to be recorded?
questions.explanation: Information can be given electronically, but it is taken on record once the informant signs it within three days.

questions.question: How does the informant or victim get a copy of the FIR?
questions.explanation: A copy of the recorded information must be given to the informant or victim forthwith, free of cost.

questions.question: Whom must the police inform when they arrest a person?
options: A relative, friend or person nominated by the arrested
questions.explanation: The police must inform a relative, friend or nominated person about the arrest and where the person is held, and also the designated police officer.

questions.question: Can a woman normally be arrested after sunset and before sunrise?
options: No, save in exceptional cases with Magistrate's permission
Yes, but only by a male officer
questions.explanation: In exceptional cases a woman police officer must make a written report and get prior permission from a Judicial Magistrate of the first class.

questions.question: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) replaced which law?
questions.explanation: The BNSS replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024. The BNS replaced the IPC and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam replaced the Evidence Act.

questions.question: Under BNSS Section 173(3), a preliminary enquiry before investigation is allowed for offences punishable with:
options: 3 years or more but less than 7 years
questions.explanation: With a DSP's prior permission, police may hold a preliminary enquiry within 14 days to see if a prima facie case exists.

questions.question: Anticipatory bail (old CrPC 438) is now provided under which BNSS section?
questions.explanation: BNSS 482 deals with bail to a person apprehending arrest. Note: BNSS 528 is the High Court's inherent power (old CrPC 482).

questions.question: Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, a confession made to a police officer:
options: Cannot be proved against the accused
questions.explanation: No confession made to a police officer can be proved against an accused (old Evidence Act s.25), to guard against forced confessions.

questions.question: Which BSA section governs admissibility of electronic records and the required certificate (old s.65B)?
questions.explanation: Section 63 sets the conditions for admitting electronic records. The certificate in the Schedule has Part A for the party and Part B for an expert.
questions.reference: Section 63(4) and Schedule, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023

questions.question: An undertrial first-time offender must be released on bond after detention for what part of the maximum sentence?
questions.explanation: Other undertrials qualify at one-half; first-time offenders at one-third. It does not apply to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.
questions.reference: Section 479(1), proviso, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

questions.question: For an offence punishable with under 3 years, DSP-level permission is needed to arrest a person who is:
options: Infirm or above 60 years of age
questions.explanation: BNSS Section 35(7) protects infirm persons and those above 60 from arrest for minor offences without prior permission of a DSP-rank officer.

questions.question: Under BNSS Section 187(3), maximum detention during investigation for offences punishable with 10 years or more is:
questions.explanation: The cap is 90 days for offences punishable with death, life or 10+ years, and 60 days for others; after that the accused gets default bail.

questions.question: Under BNSS Section 187(2), police custody of up to 15 days may be authorised:
options: Only in the first 15 days after arrest
At any stage until the trial ends
In whole or parts within the first 40 or 60 days
questions.explanation: The 15 days of police custody may be taken whole or in parts at any time during the initial 40 or 60 days of the 60/90-day detention period.

questions.question: A forensic expert must visit the crime scene for offences punishable with at least:
questions.explanation: BNSS Section 176(3) mandates a forensic team visit and videography of evidence collection for offences punishable with seven years or more.

questions.question: Where is the "discovery of fact" rule of old Evidence Act Section 27 now found?
options: Proviso to Section 23(2) of the BSA
questions.explanation: Information from an accused in police custody that leads to discovery of a fact may be proved to that extent, even if it is confessional.

questions.question: Which BSA section says no particular number of witnesses is required to prove any fact?
questions.explanation: Evidence is weighed, not counted: a single reliable witness can be enough to prove a fact (old Evidence Act s.134).

questions.question: Which BNSS section allows the trial in absentia of a proclaimed offender?
questions.explanation: Section 356 lets courts try and decide the case of a proclaimed offender who absconds to evade trial. Sections 398 and 472 deal with witness protection and mercy petitions.

questions.question: A consumer complaint where goods or services cost up to ₹50 lakh is filed before the:
questions.explanation: Under the 2021 Rules, District Commissions hear complaints where the consideration paid is up to ₹50 lakh.
questions.reference: Section 34(1), Consumer Protection Act, 2019 read with Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021

questions.question: An agreement made with a minor is:
questions.explanation: A minor is not competent to contract, so the agreement is void ab initio, as held in Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903).
questions.reference: Sections 10 and 11, Indian Contract Act, 1872; Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903) 30 IA 114

questions.question: Can a consumer file a complaint online?
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act allows complaints to be filed electronically, and consumers can file without a lawyer.

questions.question: Under the Indian Contract Act, an agreement enforceable by law is called a:
questions.explanation: Section 2(h) defines a contract as an agreement enforceable by law. Every contract is an agreement, but not every agreement is a contract.

questions.question: Within what time must a consumer complaint normally be filed?
options: 2 years from the cause of action
questions.explanation: A Consumer Commission will not admit a complaint filed after two years unless the delay is explained with sufficient cause.

questions.question: Under the Indian Contract Act, an agreement by way of wager (bet) is:
questions.explanation: Agreements by way of wager are void, and no suit can be brought to recover anything won on a bet.

questions.question: A consumer paid ₹1.5 crore for a flat. Which Commission hears the complaint?
questions.explanation: State Commissions hear complaints where consideration paid is above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore; above ₹2 crore goes to the National Commission.
questions.reference: Section 47(1)(a)(i), Consumer Protection Act, 2019 read with Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021

questions.question: A consumer complaint may be filed in the District Commission where the complainant:
options: Resides or personally works for gain
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act lets consumers sue from home: they can file where they reside or work, not only where the seller is.

questions.question: Which is an exception under Section 25 where an agreement without consideration is valid?
options: Oral promise to give a gift to a friend
Written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt
Oral promise to pay a debt not yet due
questions.explanation: Section 25(3) makes a written, signed promise to pay a debt barred by limitation enforceable even without fresh consideration.

questions.question: Which section of the Indian Contract Act deals with frustration (impossibility of performance)?
questions.explanation: A contract becomes void when performance becomes impossible or unlawful after it is made, as explained in Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur (1954).

questions.question: A person dispossessed of immovable property without due process must sue under Specific Relief Act Section 6 within:
questions.explanation: Section 6 gives a quick remedy to recover possession without proving title, but the suit must be filed within six months of dispossession.

questions.question: Section 5 of the Limitation Act (condonation of delay for sufficient cause) applies to:
questions.explanation: Delay in filing a suit cannot be condoned under Section 5; it covers appeals and applications (except under Order XXI CPC).

questions.question: After the 2018 amendment to the Specific Relief Act, specific performance of a contract is:
options: Granted only where damages are inadequate
Enforced as a rule, subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16
questions.explanation: The 2018 amendment removed judicial discretion: courts must enforce specific performance except in the cases the Act excludes.
questions.reference: Section 10, Specific Relief Act, 1963 (as substituted by Act 18 of 2018)

questions.question: Under Section 73 of the Contract Act (Hadley v. Baxendale principle), compensation is NOT given for:
options: Loss arising naturally from the breach
Loss both parties knew was likely
questions.explanation: Damages cover loss that naturally arose from the breach or that the parties knew was likely when contracting, not remote or indirect loss.

questions.question: Where a contract names a sum payable on breach, the aggrieved party under Section 74 gets:
options: Reasonable compensation up to the sum named
questions.explanation: Courts award reasonable compensation not exceeding the named sum, whether it is called a penalty or liquidated damages (Kailash Nath v. DDA, 2015).
questions.reference: Section 74, Indian Contract Act, 1872; Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA, (2015) 4 SCC 136

questions.question: Limitation for a suit for possession of immovable property based on title (Article 65) runs from adverse possession for:
questions.explanation: The owner must sue within 12 years from when the defendant's possession becomes adverse; after that the owner's right is extinguished (Section 27).
questions.reference: Article 65, Schedule, Limitation Act, 1963; Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur, (2019) 8 SCC 729

questions.question: Within how many days can an appeal be filed against a District Commission order before the State Commission?
questions.explanation: An appeal lies to the State Commission within 45 days, which it may extend for sufficient cause.

questions.question: Where both parties are mistaken about a fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is:
questions.explanation: A bilateral mistake of an essential fact makes the agreement void. A mistake by only one party does not, under Section 22.

questions.question: Under the RTI Act, a Public Information Officer must normally reply within:
questions.explanation: The PIO must provide the information or reject the request with reasons within 30 days of receiving the application.

questions.question: Which national helpline number should you call to report online financial fraud?
questions.explanation: Call 1930 quickly to help freeze the money trail, and also report on cybercrime.gov.in. 1098 is the child helpline; 112 is general emergency.
questions.reference: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in), Ministry of Home Affairs

questions.question: Under the Hindu Marriage Act, what are the minimum ages for marriage?
questions.explanation: The bridegroom must be 21 and the bride 18. Marrying below these ages is a child marriage under the 2006 Act.

questions.question: Which women are entitled to free legal services under the Legal Services Authorities Act?
options: Only women below the poverty line
questions.explanation: Section 12(c) makes every woman and child eligible for free legal aid, without an income test.

questions.question: A workplace with how many employees must form an Internal Complaints Committee under the POSH Act?
questions.explanation: Every employer with 10 or more workers must form an Internal Complaints Committee; smaller workplaces are covered by the district Local Committee.
questions.reference: Section 4(1), Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013

questions.question: What is the minimum age to get a licence to drive a private car?
questions.explanation: No one under 18 may drive a motor vehicle in a public place. At 16 one may only drive a motorcycle up to 50cc.

questions.question: If an RTI request concerns a person's life or liberty, the reply must come within:
questions.explanation: Information concerning the life or liberty of a person must be given within 48 hours of receiving the request.
questions.reference: Section 7(1), proviso, Right to Information Act, 2005

questions.question: What is the status of an award passed by a Lok Adalat?
options: Final and binding; no appeal lies
questions.explanation: A Lok Adalat award is deemed a civil court decree, is final on all parties, and cannot be appealed. Court fee paid is refunded.

questions.question: Under the DPDP Act, 2023, processing a child's personal data requires:
options: Verifiable consent of the parent or lawful guardian
Prior approval of the Data Protection Board
questions.explanation: A child is anyone under 18. Data fiduciaries must get verifiable parental consent and must not track or target ads at children.
questions.reference: Section 9, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

questions.question: Under the POSH Act, a complaint of sexual harassment should be made within:
questions.explanation: The complaint must be filed within three months of the incident (or the last one in a series); the committee may extend this by another three months.
questions.reference: Section 9(1), Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013

questions.question: Under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005, "domestic violence" includes:
options: Physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse
questions.explanation: The Act takes a wide view: depriving a woman of money or resources she is entitled to is economic abuse and counts as domestic violence.
questions.reference: Section 3, Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

questions.question: Under the Motor Vehicles Act, a Good Samaritan who helps an accident victim in good faith:
options: Is not liable to any civil or criminal action
Must pay the first hospital bill
Must give personal details to police
Must stay at the hospital till family arrives
questions.explanation: Section 134A protects good-faith helpers from liability for injury or death from emergency care, encouraging people to help victims.

questions.question: What penalty can an Information Commission impose on a PIO for unjustified delay under the RTI Act?
questions.explanation: The Commission can fine a PIO ₹250 per day of delay or obstruction, capped at ₹25,000, after giving a hearing.

questions.question: Per Vineeta Sharma (2020), a daughter's coparcenary right under amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act arises:
options: Only if father was alive on 9 Sept 2005
By birth, whether or not father was alive in 2005
questions.explanation: A three-judge bench held daughters are coparceners by birth like sons; the father need not have been alive on 9 September 2005.
questions.reference: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma, (2020) 9 SCC 1; Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956

questions.question: Per Satish Chander Ahuja (2020), a "shared household" under the DV Act can include:
options: Only a house owned by the husband
Only a house in the wife's name
In-laws' house where she lived, though owned by them
questions.explanation: The Court held a woman's right of residence extends to the household where she lived in a domestic relationship, even if owned by her in-laws.
questions.reference: Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja, (2021) 1 SCC 414; Section 2(s), Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

questions.question: Maximum DPDP Act penalty for failing to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach?
questions.explanation: The Schedule sets up to ₹250 crore for security failures; failing to notify a breach or breaching child-data duties can draw up to ₹200 crore.
questions.reference: Schedule, Item 1, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

questions.question: Which IT Act provision was struck down in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)?
questions.explanation: Section 66A (offensive online messages) was held vague and violative of Article 19(1)(a). Section 69A blocking was upheld and Section 79 read down.
questions.reference: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1

questions.question: If a juvenile commits a driving offence under the MV Act, until what age is the juvenile barred from getting a licence?
questions.explanation: Section 199A also holds the guardian or owner guilty (up to 3 years and ₹25,000 fine) and cancels the vehicle's registration.
